notes.meaning: Moses recounts how the twelve scouts set out into the mountainous region and explored the Valley of Eshcol. The valley was named for the heavy clusters of grapes the scouts discovered there.

The scouts returned to the camp bringing some of the land's rich fruit in their hands as physical proof of its abundance. They gave their report and confirmed that the territory the Lord was giving them was indeed good.
In spite of the encouraging report and the proof of the land's goodness, the people refused to march forward. Their unwillingness was open rebellion against the direct command of the Lord their God.

The Israelites retreated to their tents and grumbled against God's leadership. In their deep ingratitude, they accused the Lord of hating them and claimed He had brought them out of Egypt only to let their enemies destroy them.
The fearful report of ten of the scouts melted the courage of the entire camp. They panicked over descriptions of fortified cities with towering walls and formidable warriors known as the Anakim.
Moses tried to calm the panicked people and stop their rising fear. He pleaded with them not to be terrified or filled with dread before the inhabitants of the land.

Moses reminded the Israelites that the Lord was marching ahead of them as their true leader. He assured them that God would fight on their behalf, just as they had seen Him do during their deliverance from Egypt.

Moses pointed to their journey through the wilderness, where God tenderly provided for them at every step. The Lord had carried them through danger and hardship just as a loving father carries his own child in his arms.

Even after being reminded of God's miraculous care, the people refused to trust in the Lord. Unbelief was the real root of their disobedience, blinding them to God's past faithfulness and His dependable promises.

The Lord had faithfully traveled ahead of Israel, leading them with a pillar of fire at night and a pillar of cloud by day. He personally chose each campsite for them and marked out the safe path they were to travel.
The Lord heard the rebellious and distrustful words spoken throughout the camp. His righteous justice was provoked, and He took a solemn oath that this unfaithful generation would face judgment.

God swore that not a single person from that wicked generation would live to enter the good land. Because they refused to believe His promise, they forfeited the inheritance He had sworn to give their ancestors.
Caleb was spared from this decree because he remained completely loyal to the Lord. God promised that Caleb and his descendants would receive the land he had walked upon as an inheritance.

Moses noted that the Lord's anger also extended to him on Israel's account, preventing him from crossing into Canaan. The people's long history of bickering and rebellion provoked the incident where Moses failed to honor God properly.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical-critical scholars view these verses as a later editorial addition, suggesting Deuteronomy originally blamed Moses' exclusion on the rebellion at Kadesh rather than the later event at Meribah.

notes.meaning: God announced that Joshua, who had served as Moses' assistant, would lead the nation into Canaan. Moses was commanded to encourage Joshua so that he would boldly lead the people into their promised inheritance.

The parents had claimed their young children would become helpless plunder, but God declared those very children would enter and possess the land. Because these little ones were too young to have moral discernment during the rebellion, God spared them from their parents' punishment.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Many popular teachers use the description of children not knowing good from evil to teach an age of accountability, before which God does not hold children spiritually responsible for sin.

notes.meaning: The Lord commanded the adult generation to turn around and march away from the border of Canaan. They were ordered back into the wilderness along the route toward the Red Sea to wander until they died.

After hearing the divine sentence, the people admitted they had sinned and hastily strapped on their weapons to fight. This sudden eagerness was not true repentance, but another act of self-willed disobedience that ignored God's timing.
The Lord instructed Moses to order the people not to advance or engage in battle. Since God was no longer among them to fight for them, any military attempt would result in defeat.
Moses delivered God's warning, but the people stubbornly refused to listen. They acted presumptuously and marched up into the hills in open defiance of the Lord's clear instruction.

The Amorites living in the hill country swarmed out against the Israelites like an angry hive of bees. They chased the army down and crushed them in battle, scattering them all the way from Seir to Hormah.
The defeated Israelites came back and wept bitterly before the Lord. God refused to heed their cries because their grief was over their painful defeat rather than genuine sorrow for their sin.

Following this disastrous defeat, Israel remained camped at Kadesh for a prolonged period. Their rebellion turned what could have been a quick entry into Canaan into decades of wandering in the desert.
